title: bitwise operations, masks, and subset enumeration
concepts: Bitwise operations act independently on corresponding binary digits; AND, OR, XOR, and NOT have truth-table behavior that should be reasoned about at the bit level.
A bit mask encodes a small set using one bit per element, enabling constant-time membership tests and compact subset state when the universe fits the integer width.
Setting, clearing, toggling, and testing a bit use masks built from a one shifted to the target position; shift counts and signed integer behavior are language-specific hazards.
XOR is self-inverse, so equal values cancel in pairs and x XOR 0 equals x; these identities support parity and unique-element techniques under precise multiplicity assumptions.
The expression x AND -x isolates the least significant set bit in two's-complement integer arithmetic; clearing it with x AND (x-1) supports population-count loops.
Enumerating all subsets takes O(2^n) masks; enumerating all submasks across every mask takes O(3^n) total pairs, which is useful only for small n.
Bit tricks can reduce constants or encode state compactly, but they do not remove exponential complexity when all subsets must be considered.
Fixed-width overflow, negative values, sign extension, and shifting by the type width can invalidate informal identities; state the integer representation and constraints.

In .NET, System.Numerics.BitOperations provides current fixed-width helpers for population counts, zero counts, integer log2, power-of-two checks, rotations, and rounding up to a power of two; each API has width-specific overloads and documented zero/overflow behavior.

accuracyFacts: C# int and uint are 32-bit fixed-width types; long and ulong are 64-bit. For int/uint shifts only five low count bits are used; for long/ulong six low count bits are used.
C# signed right shift >> is arithmetic; C# 11 introduced >>> for logical right shift. Unsigned right shift fills high bits with zero.
C# bitwise and shift operations never cause overflow and produce the same results in checked and unchecked contexts; shift counts are masked to the width-specific low bits.
The one-bit mask expression 1 << 31 selects the sign bit in a 32-bit signed int; 1 << 32 shifts by zero in C# because the count is masked, so width-sized masks need explicit handling.
XOR cancellation solves the single-pair problem only when all other values have even multiplicity; XOR alone does not identify one singleton among arbitrary multiplicities.
For positive unsigned x, x & (x-1) clears the least significant 1 bit; x & -x isolates it in fixed-width two’s-complement arithmetic, but signed overflow context and minimum values require care.
Enumerating all subsets is exponential: 2^n masks; visiting all submask pairs over every mask is 3^n.
The C# unsigned right-shift operator >>> was introduced in C# 11; C# 15 is the current language version checked 2026-11-16.

The .NET 10 System.Numerics.BitOperations class includes IsPow2, LeadingZeroCount, TrailingZeroCount, Log2, PopCount, RotateLeft, RotateRight, and RoundUpToPowerOf2 overloads; it uses hardware intrinsics when available and optimized software fallbacks otherwise. Its Crc32C methods are checksum APIs and excluded from this bit-manipulation lesson.

BitOperations.LeadingZeroCount returns the fixed operand-width count when its input is zero; TrailingZeroCount does likewise for signed and unsigned overloads. Guard zero before using a count as an array/bit index.
BitOperations.Log2 returns floor(log2(value)) for positive inputs and returns 0 by convention for input 0.
BitOperations.RoundUpToPowerOf2 returns the least representable power of two greater than or equal to the input; zero input or overflow returns zero.

BigInteger bitwise operations are defined as if values use two's-complement representation with virtual sign extension; BigInteger has no fixed word width. Apply a width mask when a finite-width algorithm requires one.
BigInteger.GetBitLength returns the minimum number of bits in shortest two's-complement notation without the sign bit; it returns zero for Zero and MinusOne.
The .NET 7 generic-math interfaces IBinaryInteger<TSelf> and IBinaryNumber<TSelf> expose reusable static binary-integer operations; BigInteger implements both.
BigInteger supports the unsigned right-shift operator via its IShiftOperators implementation; its no-fixed-width representation differs from ordinary uint/ulong word semantics.
